::: {.lesson-meta}
45 minutes including the Git lab · Programming experience assumed; Git starts from first principles
:::

## What you will learn

- Distinguish working files, the staging area, and committed history.
- Use branches to develop an exclusion-rule change separately.
- Understand merges, conflicts, remotes, and pull requests.

Files named `analysis_final_really_final.py` do not tell you which rule produced a figure or why it changed. Git records a sequence of committed snapshots, together with messages and parent relationships. It lets you inspect differences and coordinate changes without silently overwriting a colleague's work.

## Git is local; GitHub hosts shared repositories

**Git** is version-control software on your computer. A **repository** contains tracked history and configuration, normally in `.git`. Your **working directory** contains the checked-out files you edit. **GitHub** hosts remote Git repositories and provides collaboration tools such as pull requests. You can commit and branch without internet or a GitHub account.

## Three places to understand

| Place | What it holds | How you inspect it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Working directory | Current files, including edits since staging | `git diff` |
| Staging area (index) | The exact proposed next snapshot | `git diff --staged` |
| Commit history | Recorded snapshots reachable through branches | `git log --oneline` |

`git add file.py` copies that file's current content into the index. If you edit again, the later edit is **unstaged** until you add it again. `git commit` records the index as a new commit and moves the current branch pointer. A commit does not automatically upload anything.

```sh
git status
git diff
git add src/experiment/preprocessing.py
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Document inclusive reaction-time bounds"
git log --oneline --graph --all
```

`git status` explains which changes are staged, unstaged, or untracked. Prefer named paths when learning so you know what enters a commit. In short status, the first column describes the index relative to HEAD; the second describes the working file relative to the index. `MM` means a file has both staged and later unstaged edits.

## Practice with five connected missions

[Open the Git practice room](../git-playground.qmd) to inspect working files, the index, HEAD, commit parents, local branches, server branches, and remote-tracking pointers. Use buttons or a bounded command console. Each mission checks the repository state you produced and includes a hint, worked route, and explanation.

1. **Stage selectively:** commit a 0.50 s rule while leaving a purple plot unstaged. Change a staged file again and explain `MM`.
2. **Merge independent work:** develop a rule on criteria and a plot on main. Identify the common ancestor before merging.
3. **Resolve deliberately:** make conflicting rules, write a resolution, stage the file, and commit. Choosing main's value still requires staging the resolution.
4. **Review and synchronize:** push a feature, review and merge a simulated PR, then fetch/pull locally. Observe how a new server commit invalidates review.
5. **Recover:** unstage without losing edits, then undo a committed change with a new inverse commit.

This simulation executes no real Git commands. Its teaching IDs such as `c0` are not hashes. It models two files, five local branches, and 50 commits; some operations are deliberately narrower than Git. Practice the same decisions in [the real Git lab](../git-lab.qmd).

## Branches and merging

A **branch** is a movable name pointing to a commit. `HEAD` normally identifies the checked-out branch. `git switch -c criteria` creates a branch at the current commit and switches to it. New commits advance that branch. `git switch main` selects main's snapshot; commit or otherwise preserve unfinished work before switching when changes would conflict.

```sh
git switch -c criteria
# edit, test, add, commit on criteria
git switch main
git merge criteria
```

If main is an ancestor of criteria, a default merge can simply move main forward: a **fast-forward**. If both branches have new commits, Git may create a merge commit with two parents. The merge base is a shared ancestor used to compare changes. A **merge conflict** means Git could not combine some edits automatically; it does not mean history has been lost. Even an automatic merge needs scientific review and tests.

For a real conflict, inspect `git status`, edit the affected file to the intended final code, remove markers, run tests, `git add` the resolved path, then `git commit`. To return to the pre-merge state while a merge is unresolved, use `git merge --abort`; start merges with a clean working tree so there is no unrelated work to recover.

## Sharing: remotes, push, pull, and review

A **remote** is a named repository location. `origin` is a conventional name, not a special kind of server. `git clone URL` downloads a repository and configures origin. `git push -u origin criteria` sends missing commits and asks the remote to update its criteria branch; `-u` records tracking information for later commands.

`git pull` fetches remote commits and integrates them into the current branch. The integration method depends on configuration. In this workshop, use `git pull --ff-only` on a clean main branch: it updates only if main can move forward without a merge or rebase. If it refuses, inspect history and coordinate instead of forcing it.

A **pull request** is a GitHub review conversation proposing to merge a source branch into a target branch. It does not exist just because you created or pushed a branch. Review the changed code, scientific rule, tests, and expected results before merging. [The Git lab](../git-lab.qmd) walks through every step on your own repository.

## Ignore local clutter; protect research inputs

`.gitignore` describes untracked paths Git should normally ignore: `.venv/`, caches, generated figures, and machine-specific settings. It does not remove already tracked files or erase history. A small synthetic teaching CSV can be committed. Sensitive participant data, credentials, and approved-storage-only datasets do not belong in a public repository.

```gitignore
.venv/
__pycache__/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
results/*
!results/.gitkeep
```

## Make the unit of review match the decision

Suppose you rename `df2` to `filtered_trials`, extract `filter_trials`, and raise the minimum RT in the same commit. A reviewer now has to distinguish an implementation change from a scientific policy change. Keep the mechanical refactor equivalent first; propose the alternative threshold in a separate config and commit.

In [the Git lab](../git-lab.qmd), add `config/rt-050.toml` and its rationale without editing the baseline or algorithm. Review whether paths point to the intended data, units are explicit, the output directory is distinct, and `run.json` records the effective settings. A pull request should explain the observed change in retained trials and estimates, not just list filenames. A clean textual merge can still combine scientifically incompatible choices.

Generated outputs are ignored here, so include a concise comparison in the review description or run notes. Keep the reproducible command and config in the commit. Never store credentials in a committed config; the filename or format does not make a value safe to share.

## Recover carefully

| Situation | Action | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staged the wrong file | `git restore --staged path` | Unstage while preserving working edits; requires an existing HEAD |
| Need to understand an old choice | `git log -- path` then `git show COMMIT:path` | Inspect history without changing current files |
| Need to undo a shared commit | `git revert COMMIT` | Create an inverse commit; review and test it |
| Unwanted uncommitted edit | First inspect `git diff -- path` | `git restore path` discards unstaged content; save a copy if uncertain |
| Sensitive file was committed | Restrict access and rotate exposed credentials | Ignoring or deleting it in a new commit does not remove old copies |

`git reflog` can help locate previous local branch positions, but it is not a backup of every uncommitted edit. Avoid force pushes and destructive resets while learning.

::: {.exercise}
<span class="exercise-label">EXERCISE 05 · A BRANCH WITH A PURPOSE</span>

### Explain the graph before pressing merge

Use mission 3 in the [practice room](../git-playground.html?mission=conflict). Before merging, identify each branch tip and their shared ancestor. Explain why changing different files would usually avoid this particular conflict. Then complete the [real local Git workflow](../git-lab.qmd).

<details><summary>Hint</summary>Creating a branch does not create a commit. Look for the last node both branch histories can reach.</details>
<details><summary>Reveal solution and explanation</summary>

With a fresh sandbox, both branches start at `c0`. Criteria's first commit is `c1`; main's is `c2`. They share `c0`. Both changed the rule from 0.20 to different values, so the merge needs a decision. Resolving creates `c3` with parents `c2` and `c1`. Changing the plot only on main and the rule only on criteria allows a clean three-way merge in this model.

</details>
:::

## Take it with you

Inspect, stage, commit, branch, and review. A commit is local; a push shares it; a pull request proposes integration. Continue to [the practical Git lab](../git-lab.qmd), then [the reproducibility handoff](06-reproducibility.qmd). References: [Git's introductory book](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2), [git restore](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-restore), and [GitHub pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests).
